title: Experimental certification of multipartite Bell correlations using only few-body symmetric correlations
authors: Jiacheng Sun, Mengyao Hu, Paweł Cieśliński, Jinfu Chen, Fei Shi, Bowen Wang, Hongyu Yang, Jizhou Wu, Jordi Tura, Valerio Scarani, Dian Wu, Jian Wu
abstract: Certifying Bell correlations in increasingly larger multipartite quantum systems is challenging because conventional Bell inequalities rely on many-body correlations, which become experimentally demanding to estimate as system size grows. Here we demonstrate that multipartite Bell correlations can be certified using few-body permutation-invariant (PI) correlations with a fixed maximal correlation order. We experimentally test few-body PI Bell correlation witnesses tailored for six- and eight-photon postselected Dicke states. The addition of a few four-body correlators is found to significantly enhance the noise tolerance compared with previously studied two-body witnesses: for instance, for six qubits, the selected witness tolerates a white-noise fraction of $p_c\approx0.301$, compared with $p_c\approx0.048$ for the best two-body PI inequality with the same two settings per party. For six and eight photons respectively, we observe violations of the witness bounds by $32$ and $8.9$ standard deviations, arising from postselected polarisation states with fidelities of $0.933(4)$ and $0.916(11)$ to the corresponding half-excitation Dicke states. The witnesses for the six- and eight-photon cases use the same symmetric two- and four-body correlators, just with different coefficients. These results demonstrate an experimentally accessible approach for certifying multipartite Bell correlations in larger systems without requiring full-body correlation measurements.
summary: This paper presents an experimental method to certify multipartite Bell correlations in large quantum systems by employing few-body symmetric correlation witnesses. By using only two- and four-body correlators, the technique overcomes the experimental difficulty associated with measuring full-body correlations as system size increases. The results confirm that this approach is robust and highly sensitive, demonstrating a scalable path for quantum verification.
main_problem: The paper addresses the experimental challenge of certifying multipartite Bell correlations in large quantum systems, where conventional methods relying on full-body correlations become experimentally intractable.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that Bell correlations can be certified using only few-body permutation-invariant (PI) correlations, significantly enhancing noise tolerance compared to using only two-body witnesses.
method: They utilize Bell correlation witnesses based on few-body PI correlators, experimentally testing these witnesses on postselected Dicke states for six- and eight-photon systems.
model_or_system: The experiments use multi-photon states, specifically six- and eight-photon postselected Dicke states, whose correlations are measured using polarization correlators.
key_observables: Bell violation factors (R), white-noise fraction tolerance ($p_c$), and measured fidelities (e.g., 0.933(4) for 6 photons).
important_parameters: System size (6 and 8 photons), correlation order (two-body and four-body), and noise tolerance thresholds.
main_assumptions: The certification characterizes the postselected ensemble, not a loophole-free test, and assumes the measured correlators are representative of the underlying state.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup for Dicke state preparation and compare measured violation factors (R) for different witnesses ($I_1, I_2, I_T$) across varying fidelities and noise levels.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of large-scale Bell certification, develops the few-body PI witness formalism, presents experimental measurements on 6- and 8-photon Dicke states, and concludes by demonstrating the enhanced noise robustness of the four-body correlators.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, experimentally accessible protocol for verifying non-classical correlations in large quantum systems by reducing the measurement burden from full-body to few-body correlations, which is highly relevant for quantum optics and quantum information.
